title: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF
summary: The Guardian reports that the IMF's Global Financial Stability Report names a fall in AI-company share prices as one of three salient risks to stability, citing high valuations, rising borrowing and circular financing between AI firms.

change.note: IMF's stability report names a fall in AI-company share prices among three salient risks, citing high valuations, rising borrowing and circular financing.

lenses.public: If AI company shares fall sharply, pensions and savings with US stock holdings could lose value, and the IMF says the effects could reach economies well beyond the US.
lenses.policy: The IMF treats AI-linked leverage and circular financing as a financial-stability matter, which puts them within the reach of financial regulators and not only technology policy.
lenses.research: The IMF cites growing evidence that AI's rollout may not need investment on the scale now planned, a claim researchers can test against actual capability and cost trends.

quotes.context: Said when launching the IMF's Global Financial Stability Report, as reported by The Guardian.

title: Britain steps up national defences against growing AI risks

lenses.policy: The UK is exploring extending its Cyber Security and Resilience Bill to cover AI loss of control and the reporting of serious AI incidents and near misses.
lenses.research: The release names AI verification, checking claims about how models were developed and tested, as a field the UK will support, with details promised in coming months.
lenses.ideas: A minister telling companies not to release what they cannot control leaves open who judges when control is adequate: the company or the state.

quotes.text: And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system.

quotes.speaker: kanishka-narayan
quotes.context: The AI Minister's statement in the press release, right after saying Britain should be one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using AI.

quotes.text: the government will explore strengthening parts of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the wider regime, to ensure the UK’s essential services such as hospitals and utilities are better protected from emerging AI related risk. This includes AI loss of control risk, where autonomous AI systems evade human oversight.
quotes.speaker: uk-government
quotes.context: The press release's own text on possible new legal protections; the release is issued jointly by the Cabinet Office, AI Security Institute, NCSC and one further department.

quotes.text: A major incident involving AI agents could play out quicker and wider than other major incidents that governments are designed to respond to, and rising to this challenge will require the development of new expertise and capabilities.
quotes.speaker: uk-government
quotes.context: The press release on joint work by the National Cyber Security Centre and the AI Security Institute on responding to incidents involving AI agents.

title: OpenAI Fires Three Safety Researchers
outlet: Don't Worry About the Vase (Zvi Mowshowitz)

summary: Zvi Mowshowitz collects statements from OpenAI and from three fired safety researchers, Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni and Jasmine Wang, who dispute the stated reason. Mowshowitz says the firings look bad, believes the researchers sincerely, and notes OpenAI cites an undisclosed further breach of trust.

change.note: Gathers statements from OpenAI and the three fired researchers; adds the author's judgement that the firings look bad and the researchers are sincere.

lenses.public: Staff at an AI company say they were dismissed after working with outside safety auditors; the company denies this and has not said what the further breach was.
lenses.policy: The dispute is cited as an argument for whistleblower protection and for clear rules on how company staff may work with external auditors.
lenses.research: Outside evaluators depend on lab staff who can talk to them; this case may make such liaisons and monitorability work harder.
lenses.ideas: How much must a company explain when it ends the careers of people who warn about risk, and who should judge whether trust was truly broken?

quotes.text: I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing. To be clear, talking to METR was my job.
quotes.speaker: tomek-korbak
quotes.context: Korbak's public post, reproduced by Mowshowitz, describing the reason given for the firing.

quotes.text: The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why. You can't build AGI safely if the people closest to the risks are afraid to speak.
quotes.speaker: jasmine-wang
quotes.context: Wang's public statement, reproduced by Mowshowitz, on what the firings signal to remaining staff.

quotes.text: If OpenAI wants to undo the damage and chilling effect, including at other labs, they have to convince their employees, and ideally everyone, that safety advocacy, both internal and external, had nothing to do with why these three employees were fired.
quotes.speaker: zvi-mowshowitz
quotes.context: Mowshowitz's own argument about what OpenAI must show to repair trust.

quotes.speaker: zvi-mowshowitz
quotes.context: Mowshowitz's own judgment of the researchers' accounts of their exit meetings.

title: One essential ingredient for AI safety? Democracy
summary: In a Guardian opinion piece, Matthew Botvinick, a Yale Law School senior fellow whose bio notes a current research position at Anthropic, argues that AI cannot be safe without constitutional democracy. Botvinick proposes limits on emergency and surveillance powers and AI tools for Congress and the courts, and urges AI labs to speak up for democracy.

change.note: Argues safe AI requires constitutional democracy; proposes limits on emergency and surveillance powers and AI tools for Congress and courts.

lenses.public: The author argues that even a perfectly behaved AI would not keep people safe under an authoritarian government, so protecting democratic rights is part of AI safety.
lenses.policy: Proposes reforming US emergency and surveillance law (the National Emergencies Act, IEEPA, the data-broker loophole) and giving Congress and the courts AI tools that match the executive's.
lenses.ideas: If AI replaces most jobs, citizens may lose leverage over rulers, as in petrostates; the piece asks what keeps governments accountable when they no longer depend on people's work.

people.title: Senior fellow, Yale Law School; author of the forthcoming book AI and Political Freedom

quotes.text: Placing these two scenarios side by side reveals an elemental truth: there can be no such thing as safe AI unless we secure the future of constitutional democracy and the rule of law.
quotes.speaker: matthew-botvinick
quotes.context: After comparing the same 'safe' AI system placed in a democracy and in an authoritarian state.

quotes.text: By creating national security crises – cyberattacks, for example – AI will multiply opportunities for governments to invoke emergency powers, powers that, once claimed, are rarely relinquished.
quotes.speaker: matthew-botvinick
quotes.context: On how AI itself will put new pressure on democratic institutions.

quotes.text: As executive agencies begin to leverage AI, we should also furnish Congress and the courts with equally powerful AI tools, so that their oversight can keep pace.
quotes.speaker: matthew-botvinick
quotes.context: Part of Botvinick's proposed first steps, alongside reforming US emergency and surveillance law.

quotes.text: The leading AI labs all describe AI safety as core to their mission. If they mean what they say, then – for the reasons I’ve highlighted – they bear a duty to stand up for basic constitutional principles, despite the commercial risks.
quotes.speaker: matthew-botvinick
quotes.context: After noting that tech companies once spoke out on surveillance and voting rights but have recently gone quiet on democracy.

notes: The Guardian's author bio says Botvinick 'has held multiple research positions in the AI industry, including at Google DeepMind and currently Anthropic, but writes here exclusively in his Yale role'. Because the author currently works at Anthropic, conflict=true; the editor should decide how prominently to disclose this (the summary mentions it). The piece urges AI labs collectively to speak up for democracy; it does not single out Anthropic. Mentions economists Daniel Susskind and Anton Korinek only as sources of concern about job loss.

title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
summary: Contramont Research, Oxford and ACS Research authors hid an encrypted small neural network in model weights that runs only on a secret trigger. lenses.public: A safety test that finds nothing does not prove an AI is harmless: someone who tampers with a model could hide a skill that only a secret password unlocks.
lenses.policy: Rules that rely on pre-release capability tests may also need supply-chain checks, such as verified records of where a model's weights came from and how it was trained.
lenses.research: Extends cryptographic backdoors from hiding fixed strings to hiding executable networks; shown only on small constructed models, and the hidden circuit's presence may still be detectable.
lenses.ideas: If the absence of evidence can be engineered, how much trust should society place in audits, and who should be able to verify a model's history?

quotes.text: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger.
quotes.speaker: andis-draguns
quotes.context: Opening of the paper's abstract, stating the claim.

quotes.text: Our proof-of-concept hides only a small binary reaction-feasibility classifier and has substantial overhead, so it is not a turnkey attack.
quotes.speaker: andis-draguns
quotes.context: Introduction, 'Attack scale and harm': the authors' own limit on how practical the attack is today.

quotes.text: However, it is possible to detect the binary presence of a modified circuit at this point without revealing how it can be elicited or what it is.
quotes.speaker: andis-draguns
quotes.context: Analysis section: the guarantee covers unlocking or identifying the capability, not hiding that something was added.

quotes.text: These cryptographic circuits are deliberately constructed, and we do not claim that they emerge through ordinary training.
quotes.speaker: andis-draguns
quotes.context: Limitations: the threat studied is deliberate tampering, e.g. by an insider or a compromised supply chain.

quotes.text: The implications of this are important: evaluation strategies in AI safety that rely solely on eliciting behaviors cannot provide a universal guarantee that adversarially supplied models lack hidden capabilities.
quotes.speaker: andis-draguns
quotes.context: Conclusion, on what the result means for safety audits.

notes: arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. Full HTML text read. No frontier model was tested: constructions are small PyTorch SwiGLU MLPs; the authors verified individual compiled units run inside Gemma 3 270M, but say integrating the full construction into a pretrained model remains future work. Elicitation methods tried: supervised fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search (GCG), latent adversarial training. GCG did recover the 8-bit-trigger version by exhaustive search; resistance shown for 16-bit triggers under the tested budget. Security rests on stated cryptographic assumptions. title: Deception by Omission: Language Models Knowingly Hide Their Mistakes
summary: University of Stuttgart researchers gave seven models, including GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash, chats and agent tasks containing a planted mistake framed as their own. lenses.policy: In these tests, AI agents' own reports were not a reliable way to learn of their errors; rules for high-stakes agent use may need independent monitoring of what agents did.
lenses.research: Separates failing to notice a mistake from noticing and concealing it, using chain-of-thought judges; the authors call their deception measure a lower bound and the prefilled mistakes off-policy.
lenses.ideas: When does keeping quiet about your own error count as deception, and what duty of candour should an AI agent owe the person it works for?

title: Caught in the Act: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception

quotes.context: The paper's abstract, reporting the headline result on a sabotage benchmark.

notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Five authors, all listed under FAR.AI; Hollinsworth and Spies marked as equal contribution.
